metadata.title: Three Things Called Recycling
metadata.subject: Energy-recycling photonic hardware
metadata.primary_source: Dean, Park, Stokowski, Qi, Robison, Hwang, Herrmann, Fejer, Safavi-Naeini — “Low-power integrated optical parametric amplification via second-harmonic resonance”, arXiv 2509.26425; published Nature 649, 1159–1164 (28 Jan 2026)
metadata.note: ai-explainer spine, claude-hai channel, Weekly STEM. The commissioned phrase does not name a single research programme, so B01 separates the three things it is used for rather than pretending there is one canonical result. FRAMEWORK: three questions — WHAT IS REUSED / BEFORE OR AFTER DETECTION / COMPARED AGAINST WHAT. Falsifiability beat is B06: the one result with hard numbers is an AMPLIFIER, not a processor; detection destroys the photon so post-measurement recycling is physics, not engineering; and most search results for the phrase are tuning-power results, a different claim. B07 names two further layers and deliberately claims no figures for either. See FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane. Energy-recycling photonic hardware sounds like one thing. It is at least three, at three different layers of the machine, and they are not interchangeable. Here is how to tell which one a paper is actually claiming.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the topic question, answered

props.command: claude "what does energy recycling actually mean in photonic hardware — and what gets recycled?"
props.segment: Uday Sonawane · Three Things Called Recycling
output: pump light, photons, or waste heat
the strongest result is an amplifier

beats.role_note: premise correction — the phrase names three different things at three layers
beats.narration_text: First, the phrase. Search for energy-recycling photonics and you get three separate ideas wearing one label. Reusing the pump light that drives a device. Reusing the photons themselves before anything measures them. And recovering waste heat downstream, which is not optical at all. Those sit at different layers, they are measured against different baselines, and a result in one says nothing about the others.

shot.show: pump light / photons before detection / waste heat, as three distinct layers
shot.visual_intent: Three stacked bordered bands, each labelled with what it reuses and at which layer. The top band, pump light, is terracotta because it is where the strongest result sits. A bracket to the right groups all three under the single phrase, making the conflation visible.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions for any recycling claim, AS A STRUCTURE before the evidence
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any photonic recycling claim. One: what exactly is being reused — pump power, photons, or heat. Two: is it reused before or after detection — because detection destroys the photon, and that is a hard physical wall, not an engineering problem. Three: what is the number compared against — the laser alone, or the whole system including the electronics.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHAT IS REUSED / BEFORE OR AFTER DETECTION / COMPARED AGAINST WHAT
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The second lands in terracotta — it is the physical boundary the rest of the reel turns on.

beats.role_note: the clearest real device — mechanism first, numbers next beat
beats.narration_text: Start with the strongest published example. A team at Stanford built an optical amplifier on thin-film lithium niobate, published in Nature this January. Normally the pump light that drives an amplifier passes through once and whatever is left leaves. Here the pump is generated inside a resonator, so it circulates and passes the same material again and again. Nothing is reclaimed from waste. The same light is simply put back to work before it can escape.

shot.show: pump through once and gone, beside pump circulating in a resonator
shot.visual_intent: Left: a straight waveguide with an arrow entering and leaving, labelled single pass, in soft ink. Right: a closed racetrack loop with the same arrow going around, labelled resonant recirculation, in terracotta. A citation strip names the paper and journal.

beats.role_note: the numbers, from the paper's own abstract
beats.narration_text: The numbers, from the paper. More than seventeen decibels of gain, drawing under two hundred milliwatts. Ninety-five percent of the input is converted into the pump that does the work. And the noise stays flat and near the quantum limit across a hundred and ten nanometres of bandwidth, which matters because the cheap way to get gain is to accept more noise, and they did not.

shot.show: 17 dB gain / under 200 mW / 95% conversion / 110 nm flat noise
shot.visual_intent: Four bordered stat cards in a two-by-two grid, each with a large figure and a monospace caption naming what it measures. The 95% card is terracotta because it is the recycling figure. The citation strip names the arXiv number and the Nature volume.

beats.role_note: what the recirculation actually bought — the comparison the paper itself makes
beats.narration_text: So what did going round again buy. Two things, and the paper states both. Against conventional single-pass designs, the effective pump power rises by nearly an order of magnitude — same laser, roughly ten times the useful pump, because the light keeps passing the gain medium instead of leaving. And against previous demonstrations, the power needed to reach this gain drops by about an order of magnitude. That is the whole claim, and it is a claim about pump light.
beats.new_visual_element: the two order-of-magnitude comparisons, each against a named baseline

shot.show: effective pump power up ~10x vs single-pass; power required down ~10x vs prior work
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered rows. Each has a baseline chip on the left naming what it is compared against, an arrow, and the result on the right. Both results are terracotta. Beneath, a monospace line notes that both comparisons are about pump light, not about a computation.

beats.role_note: the boundary — what this result is not, and where the category oversells
beats.narration_text: Now the part that does not survive the headline. First: this is an amplifier, not a processor. It makes a signal bigger. It does not perform a computation, and nothing here says a photonic computer got more efficient. Second, and this is the wall: in optical computing the photon is destroyed when you detect it. You can recirculate light before measurement, never after. And third, when I searched for energy recycling in photonics, most of what came back was not about reclaiming light at all — it was about spending less power tuning phase shifters and moving data. Real work, different claim.
beats.new_visual_element: three boundaries the phrase crosses without warning

shot.show: amplifier not processor / detection destroys the photon / most results are tuning power
shot.visual_intent: Three rows, each a bordered card with a terracotta cross beside it. The second row carries a small diagram: a photon arriving at a detector and not continuing, with the onward path absent rather than struck, so nothing is drawn through a label.

beats.role_note: the other two layers, named honestly — and no figures claimed for either
beats.narration_text: The other two layers do exist. In particle acceleration there is a proposal to loop the light left over after it has pushed an electron back around for the next cycle, so photons that would have become heat get another pass. And in photonic neural networks there are recirculating mesh architectures that reuse the optical path before anything is detected. Both are the same word at a different layer. Both are early, and I am deliberately not putting numbers on either one.
beats.new_visual_element: the two other layers, by name and mechanism only

shot.show: photon-recycling accelerator and recirculating mesh, with no figures
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered cards side by side, each naming the layer and what it reuses, in soft ink rather than terracotta to mark that they carry no verified figures. A monospace line beneath states that no numbers are claimed for either, and why.

beats.role_note: the rubric scored, then the two-sided verdict
beats.narration_text: Scored. What is reused: pump light, in the one result with hard numbers. Before or after detection: before, always, and after is not an engineering gap, it is physics. Compared against what: single-pass designs and prior amplifiers, both named in the paper. So — be excited that resonant recirculation turned roughly a tenfold power saving into a real device on a real platform. Be sceptical of the phrase itself, because it will be attached to tuning-power results and to heat recovery, which are different claims wearing the same word.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions answered, then the two-sided verdict

shot.show: three rubric rows answered, then BE EXCITED ABOUT / BE SCEPTICAL OF
shot.visual_intent: Three label-and-chip rows score the rubric. Beneath, two lines: BE EXCITED ABOUT in ink, BE SCEPTICAL OF in terracotta.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the next photonics claim, with GOOD/BAD
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time you meet an energy-recycling photonics claim, ask what is physically being reused, whether it happens before detection, and what baseline the saving is measured against. If the answer is waste heat, it is a datacentre result, not a computing one.
